name: Hassan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run blast-hole drill rigs at the Copper Ridge open pit. These days I don't sit in one rig, I sit in a cab on the bench with a laptop and supervise two semi-automatic rigs at once, plus my own. Each rig drills holes about fifteen metres deep in a grid, so the blasting crew can load them with explosives. I start at six, check the drill plan the engineers sent overnight, and then spend the day watching the rigs, fixing their mistakes and swapping worn bits. I love it when the pattern comes out perfect, and I hate the dust storms in August that shut everything down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned a laptop. How much do you use technology in the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use an AI assistant to read through the rig manufacturer's manuals, to sort out fault codes and to write my end-of-shift report in half the time. I'm also on the union's technology committee, the one that sits with management when they bring in new systems. My wife Meena works at the pharmacy in town, our daughter Priya tests software overseas, and our son Ravi is a chef. They tease me that I'm the oldest nerd on the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's a bit disappointing. I'd still tell people AI is a good tool, because it saves me forty minutes a shift already. On the union chat, I'd say let's make sure the time it saves goes to workers, not just to the bottom line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep doing what I'm doing, and I'm quite good at it. I'd miss the excitement a bit, because I like learning new systems. But my job is safe to sixty-five, and that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd keep running my rigs, keep using the AI assistant for reports and faults, and keep showing the younger drillers how to use it. Meena and I would keep putting about four hundred a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. Like a film where the big ending never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the saved time should go to workers. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shorter week, or at least no extra tasks loaded on because the reports are quicker. Last year they saved us time with a new scheduling system and then just added more holes per shift. I argued at the committee and lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew uses these tools least?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bongani, who's been drilling as long as I have. He's brilliant with a rig but he won't touch a phone app. I'd keep sitting with him at lunch and showing him one thing at a time.

S0.say: It's a bit disappointing, but AI is still a good tool that saves me forty minutes a shift. Let's make sure the time it saves goes to workers, not just the bottom line.
S0.think: I keep doing what I'm good at, and my job is safe to sixty-five. I'd miss the excitement of new systems a little, but that's not nothing.
S0.do: Keeps running the rigs and using the AI assistant for reports and faults. Keeps coaching younger drillers and colleagues like Bongani, and keeps saving about four hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, like a film without its big ending.
S0.quote: Like a film where the big ending never comes.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan is the rare senior miner who is genuinely excited by new tools, so the plateau almost disappoints him. His progressive streak shows in his focus on who keeps the saved time. He is patient and generous with less tech-minded colleagues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what we've been preparing for on the technology committee. The rigs get smarter, and the people who drill get trained to run them, not replaced. I'd write it up for the union newsletter with real examples from our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I come out ahead. I already run three rigs from one cab, and in a few years it might be ten from a control room. Somebody has to understand the rock and the machine, and I'm one of the few who knows both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to help commission the next generation of autonomous rigs, so I'm the one who writes the procedures. I'd push the committee for paid training for every driller, not just the keen ones. And I'd keep learning, maybe a short online course in automation systems over winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, if I'm truthful. I know that's not how most of my mates would feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Bongani in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my worry. He's fifty-six and he won't learn a new screen without someone holding his hand. I'd fight for him to get a role on the bench changing bits and doing maintenance, which still needs a person for a while yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the company would do that you'd push against?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Using the new rigs to cut crews before anyone's trained. They'd try it, they always try it. I'd say no automation goes in without a training plan signed off by the committee.

S1.say: This is what we've prepared for on the technology committee: the rigs get smarter and the drillers get trained to run them, not replaced.
S1.think: I think I come out ahead, because I already run three rigs from one cab. Somebody has to understand the rock and the machine, and I'm one of the few who knows both.
S1.do: Volunteers to help commission the next autonomous rigs and write the procedures. Pushes for paid training for every driller and takes a short online automation course over winter.
S1.feel: Calm and somewhat excited, while aware most mates wouldn't feel the same.
S1.quote: Somebody has to understand the rock and the machine, and I'm one of the few who knows both.
S1.fieldNote: Hassan sees steady change as his moment and is honest that he'd benefit. His concern shifts quickly to colleagues like Bongani who won't adapt easily. He mixes eager adoption with firm union lines about training before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the gains from this have to be shared, and fast, because there's no time for the usual slow fight. A robot dividend, a shorter week, a public fund, something. I'd say that everywhere, online included, and I'd be at the union's door the first day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with technology doesn't help if the technology doesn't need me. If AI can run a whole drill fleet and robots can change the bits, my place in the cab disappears too. I'd be sixty with maybe four months saved, which isn't a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd offer myself as a commissioning hand to every mine in the region that's switching over, because for a year or two they'll need people who know both sides. I'd bank every cent of that and cut back at home. And I'd push the union and our local member hard for a public income for displaced workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can still see a couple of moves, but the board is shrinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You love new technology. Does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and that's the strange part. I'd still find it amazing to watch. I'd just be watching it from my kitchen instead of from the cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya, who works in software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her what she's hearing, because she'd know before me. And I'd tell her not to be proud about moving home if she has to. We'd squeeze in, Meena and I already talked about the spare room once.

S2.say: The gains have to be shared, and fast, because there's no time for the usual slow fight. A robot dividend, a shorter week or a public fund.
S2.think: Being good with technology doesn't help if the technology doesn't need me. I'd be sixty with maybe four months saved, which isn't a plan.
S2.do: Offers himself as a commissioning hand to mines switching to automation in the region and banks every cent of it. Cuts back at home and pushes the union and his local member for a public income for displaced workers.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a few moves left but a shrinking board.
S2.quote: I'd still find it amazing to watch. I'd just be watching it from my kitchen instead of from the cab.
S2.fieldNote: Even an adaptive worker runs out of road when the end point arrives this fast, and Hassan says so plainly. He finds a short-term angle as a commissioning hand, which shows his instinct to move first. His fascination with the technology survives his own loss, which was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to write the rules, and the unions should be at the table writing them, not reacting. I'd want automation levies to fund retraining and an early pension option for older miners. I'd speak at the regional union conference about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to ride the wave. I'd move into the automation team and probably stay useful until about 2030. After that I'm sixty-two and very close to the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to move from the drill bench to the site automation team in the first year, even if it's the same pay. I'd grow savings to about eight months by putting away the extra overtime that commissioning brings. And I'd keep pushing the levy and early pension idea through the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good-tension way. Like the start of a long drill pattern.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you compared with 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to be the one doing the change instead of having it done to me. In 2028 I'm scrambling for short contracts. In 2031 I'm on the team, I have a title, and I go out on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you be worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young drillers who just signed on, like Thabo, who's twenty-three. In five years he's twenty-eight and trained for a job that's vanishing. I'd tell him to come with me onto the automation team now.

S3.say: We have five years to write the rules, and the unions should be at the table writing them, with automation levies for retraining and an early pension option for older miners.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to ride the wave. I'd move into the automation team, stay useful until about 2030, and by then I'm close to the line.
S3.do: Moves from the drill bench to the site automation team in the first year. Builds savings to about eight months from commissioning overtime and pushes the levy and early pension idea through the union.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but with a useful kind of tension.
S3.quote: In 2028 I'm scrambling for short contracts. In 2031 I'm on the team, I have a title, and I go out on my own terms.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time lets Hassan's adaptability do real work for him: he can lead the change rather than chase it. He thinks clearly about timing relative to his own retirement. His concern for young workers like Thabo is concrete and practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this well, and there's no excuse for anyone in our industry to be left behind. Every miner should get paid training and a say in how the robots come in. I'd keep saying that on the committee and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd retire around 2033 having spent my last years building the system that replaces my old job, which I'd actually enjoy. My worry is only whether the money from all this ends up anywhere near towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and keep helping commission each new rig as it comes. I'd spend evenings on online courses in automation and keep using AI for everything I can. And I'd campaign for a regional fund from mining royalties, so the town still has a future after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about it, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd enjoy building the system that replaces your job. Does that ever feel odd?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, like teaching your replacement on your last day. But better I teach it than someone who's never stood on a bench in a dust storm. At least it'll know what the rock's like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ravi, the chef?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cook while people still want a person in the kitchen, and learn the business side. He's twenty-nine, so 2036 is right in the middle of his life. I'd tell him to save more than I did, honestly.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to do this well, and there's no excuse for anyone in our industry to be left behind. Every miner should get paid training and a say in how the robots come in.
S4.think: For me it's fine: I'd retire around 2033 after building the system that replaces my old job, and I'd enjoy it. My only worry is whether the money ends up anywhere near towns like ours.
S4.do: Keeps drilling while helping commission each new rig. Studies automation online in the evenings, uses AI wherever he can, and campaigns for a regional fund from mining royalties.
S4.quote: Better I teach it than someone who's never stood on a bench in a dust storm.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade's notice Hassan is relaxed, even enthusiastic, and his worry becomes about where the profits go. He admits he wishes he had saved more, which he passes on as advice to his son. His mix of tech enthusiasm and union politics is consistent throughout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I can adapt to almost anything given a couple of years, but not to being unnecessary at sixty with four months in the bank. What would help is a public income that kicks in when your job's automated, paid for by the companies doing the automating.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. That's the whole question for me. If the drill rigs were owned partly by the people who used to drive them, I'd be cheering for all five of your pictures.

headlineQuote: If the drill rigs were owned partly by the people who used to drive them, I'd be cheering for all five of your pictures.
portrait: Hassan Patel is a 58-year-old blast-hole drill operator at an open-pit copper mine who already supervises several semi-automatic rigs and uses AI every day. He sits on the union's technology committee and believes the gains from automation should be shared with workers. He is calm through the plateau and steady change, sees himself leading the shift, and stays calm or merely uneasy with five or ten years' warning. Only AGI in two years makes him anxious, because his adaptability can't help if he's no longer needed at sixty.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd be unnecessary at sixty with only about four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A public income that starts when a job is automated, funded by the companies doing the automating.
